annotations.organization: Use a tailored arc42 organization. Preserve an adequate project layout by mapping these topics to its headings; consolidate related sections when useful.
annotations.completeness: Account for every topic with evidence. Distinguish implemented facts, accepted target design, assumptions, and unverified coverage. Conditional topics may be inapplicable only with a reason.
annotations.diagrams: The required, optional, and unnecessary criteria below are this skill's tailoring policy. Include a view only when it materially improves explanation; use prose for trivial relationships. Keep names, boundaries, directions, protocols, cardinality, and runtime ordering consistent with prose and evidence. Give each diagram a title stating its type and scope and a legend; label element types, responsibilities, and relationship intent, with technologies and protocols at the appropriate abstraction level.
annotations.c4_defaults: Treat system context, container, and deployment views as C4-recommended defaults. Omit one only when the document records why its intended readers and scope do not benefit; component, dynamic, and code views remain value-driven.
annotations.limits: Mechanical validation checks declarations and syntax only. Section presence, declared coverage, link existence, and rendered Mermaid never prove architectural quality, behavioral truth, security, or complete review.
annotations.references: The wording and template are original. IEEE 1016-2009 is an inactive-reserved historical completeness reference; its public official scope supports design information and stakeholder communication. The licensed full text was not inspected, so do not assert clause-level conformance.

sections.heading: 1 Purpose and goals
sections.content: State purpose, scope, stakeholders, intended readers, prerequisite knowledge, goals, and non-goals; identify the design questions readers must decide and prioritize the architectural quality goals that drive them.

sections.heading: 2 Constraints and assumptions
sections.content: Separate imposed constraints from assumptions; give assumptions an owner or a way to verify them.

sections.heading: 3 System context
sections.content: Describe the system boundary, users, external dependencies, trust boundaries, and the responsibilities on each side.

sections.heading: 4 Solution strategy
sections.content: Explain the approach, its important tradeoffs, and how it supports goals under the constraints.

sections.heading: 5 Building blocks
sections.content: Identify major applications, stores, modules, responsibilities, interfaces, and implementation locations at useful levels of detail.

sections.heading: 6 Runtime behavior
sections.content: Explain important successful and failing sequences, state changes, concurrency, retry or idempotency behavior, and recovery when relevant.

sections.heading: 7 Deployment and operations
sections.content: Map executable units to environments and infrastructure; cover configuration, rollout, observability, and operational ownership. For a library or local tool, state its host/runtime expectations.

sections.heading: 8.1 Data and persistence
sections.content: When state is managed, explain the data model, persistence, schema authority, lifecycle, migration, compatibility, and rollback or irreversible transitions.

sections.heading: 8.2 APIs and integrations
sections.content: When interfaces exist, link their authoritative contracts and describe authentication, payloads, errors, versioning, timeouts, and compatibility obligations.

sections.heading: 8.3 Security and resilience
sections.content: Assess security, privacy, reliability, backup, and recovery applicability individually; describe relevant trust and access controls, sensitive data handling, failure containment, retention, restore objectives, and evidence. Do not waive this whole topic merely because one part is inapplicable.

sections.heading: 9 Decisions and alternatives
sections.content: Record consequential architectural decisions, status, reasoning, and rejected alternatives; link accepted ADRs without duplicating their authority.

sections.heading: 10 Quality scenarios
sections.content: Define measurable scenarios with stimulus, operating conditions, affected element, expected response, threshold, and verification method; distinguish desired targets from measured results.

sections.heading: 11 Risks and limitations
sections.content: Record concrete risks, technical debt, known limitations, consequence, mitigation or acceptance, and ownership; do not silently treat unknown behavior as supported.

sections.heading: 12 Glossary and references
sections.content: Define domain terms and link authoritative references. Use one identity for each architectural element across prose, diagrams, and implementation.

sections.heading: 13 Testing and verification
sections.content: Map material design claims and quality scenarios to behavior tests, integration or migration checks, operational evidence, and remaining verification gaps.

sections.heading: 14 Ownership and maintenance
sections.content: Name the document owner, authoritative path, source-of-truth hierarchy, and update triggers. Explain how code, APIs, data, deployment, decisions, and quality changes trigger a design review.

views.title: C4 system landscape
views.required_when: The document covers a portfolio or organisation and cross-system ownership or dependencies cannot be understood from per-system context views.
views.optional_when: Several peer systems benefit from one shared portfolio map.
views.unnecessary_when: The document concerns one software system and its external dependencies are clear in its system-context view.

views.title: C4 system context
views.required_when: Multiple actors or external systems, or a significant trust or ownership boundary, make a prose-only account ambiguous.
views.optional_when: One simple external interaction still benefits stakeholder communication.
views.unnecessary_when: The system is isolated or its boundary and single interaction are already clear in concise prose.

views.title: C4 container
views.required_when: Several applications or stores interact and the distribution of responsibilities or communication materially affects the design.
views.optional_when: A simple application/store split is useful to the intended readers.
views.unnecessary_when: One executable unit has no meaningful internal application/store split; a C4 container is not synonymous with a Docker container.

views.title: C4 component
views.required_when: A critical internal boundary or collaboration inside one container cannot be adequately explained by its container view and prose.
views.optional_when: A stable internal decomposition helps developers make an actual design decision.
views.unnecessary_when: It would restate file lists or code structure without explaining a consequential relationship.

views.title: C4 code
views.required_when: A critical implementation structure cannot be adequately explained at component level and the view can be generated from authoritative source.
views.optional_when: An important complex area benefits from a generated class, entity, or dependency view.
views.unnecessary_when: For ordinary code structure or whenever a hand-maintained diagram would duplicate source code.

views.title: C4 deployment
views.required_when: Distribution, environment differences, replication, failover, or a network/trust boundary materially affects operation.
views.optional_when: A simple host/runtime mapping benefits operators.
views.unnecessary_when: A local tool or library has one obvious host arrangement adequately stated in prose.

views.title: C4 dynamic or sequence
views.required_when: Ordering, concurrency, asynchronous handoff, retry, transaction boundaries, or recovery has consequential interactions that prose cannot explain clearly.
views.optional_when: A recurring user journey benefits from a compact ordered interaction view.
views.unnecessary_when: The operation is a trivial linear call or would duplicate an already sufficient sequence. Use one notation per scenario.
